required_tasks: Formulate a unit-consistent elevator-and-rocket transport model.
Find all nominal optima at elevator cost 900 per tonne.
Find optima at both endpoint elevator costs 700 and 1400 per tonne.
Find every optimal-plan switching value in [700,1400] and all tied plans.
Provide a standard-library Python solver using the supplied function signature and arguments.
Provide a directly insertable LaTeX body fragment.
Write a 130-190 word letter to the logistics manager.
optional_tasks: Model stochastic rocket or elevator failures; not pursued because no failure probabilities were supplied.
transport.uncertainty_kind: Deterministic sensitivity to elevator cost per tonne; no probabilistic uncertainty is modeled.
transport.solver_notes: Exact nonintegral values are represented as strings in numerator/denominator form, so the switching price is 10000/9 and each tied total cost is 370000/9; integral results are JSON integers. The solver converts inputs to Fraction, converts 9000 kg to 9 tonnes, and compares costs exactly, so no floating-point tie tolerance is needed. Passing the switch as a numerator/denominator string or as a Fraction preserves exactness; a finite decimal input is interpreted as its decimal literal. In the parameter range, candidate costs are 19c+20000, 10c+30000, c+40000, and 50000. The only in-range lower-envelope crossing is 10000/9; the other pairwise crossings, 30000/19, 2000, and 10000, are outside [700,1400]. At the switch, the n=5 zero-elevator plan costs 50000 and does not tie.
transport.latex_model:
Let \(D=37\,\mathrm{t}\), \(\bar E=20\,\mathrm{t}\), \(R=9000\,\mathrm{kg}=9\,\mathrm{t}\), and \(F=10000\) currency units per launch. Let \(c\) be the elevator price in currency units per tonne. The decisions are elevator tonnage \(e\) and integer launch count \(n\). The unit-consistent model is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{e,n}\quad & C(e,n)=ce+Fn,\\
\text{s.t.}\quad & e+Rn\ge D,\\
&0\le e\le\bar E,\\
&n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The inequality permits unused rocket capacity. Since \(c>0\), excess elevator tonnage cannot reduce cost, so for fixed feasible \(n\),
\[
e(n)=\max\{0,D-Rn\}.
\]
The elevator cap requires \(n\ge2\), while \(n>5\) only adds fixed cost. The relevant plans are
\[
(e,n)\in\{(19,2),(10,3),(1,4),(0,5)\},
\]
with costs
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_2(c)&=19c+20000, & C_3(c)&=10c+30000,\\
C_4(c)&=c+40000, & C_5(c)&=50000.
\end{aligned}
\]
At \(c=900\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_2&=37100, & C_3&=39000,\\
C_4&=40900, & C_5&=50000.
\end{aligned}
\]
so the unique nominal optimum is \((e,n)=(19,2)\). At \(c=700\), the unique optimum is also \((19,2)\) with cost \(33300\). At \(c=1400\), the unique optimum is \((1,4)\) with cost \(41400\).

The lower-envelope crossing satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
19c+20000&=10c+30000,\\
10c+30000&=c+40000,
\end{aligned}
\]
so
\[
c^*=\frac{10000}{9}\approx1111.11.
\]
At \(c^*\),
\[
C_2=C_3=C_4=\frac{370000}{9},
\]
and the tied plans are
\[
(e,n)\in\{(19,2),(10,3),(1,4)\}.
\]
Thus two launches are optimal for \(700\le c<c^*\), all three plans tie at \(c^*\), and four launches are optimal for \(c^*<c\le1400\).
transport.summary: We formulate elevator-and-rocket delivery as a mixed-integer cost minimization problem. Demand is 37 tonnes; the elevator can carry 20 tonnes, each launch can carry 9 tonnes, elevator freight costs c per tonne, and each launch costs 10,000. At the nominal c=900, the unique optimum uses 19 elevator tonnes and two launches, costing 37,100. Across c from 700 to 1,400, the endpoint optima are two launches and 19 tonnes at 33,300, then four launches and one tonne at 41,400. The exact switch is 10,000/9: below it two launches are optimal, there three plans tie, and above it four launches are optimal.
transport.letter:
Dear Logistics Manager,

For the 37-tonne requirement, I recommend two rocket launches and 19 tonnes by elevator at the nominal rate of 900 per tonne. This meets demand exactly, leaves one tonne of elevator capacity unused, and costs 37,100 currency units. The alternative with three launches costs 39,000, and four launches costs 40,900.

The recommendation is sensitive to the elevator price. At 700 per tonne, two launches and 19 elevator tonnes still minimize cost at 33,300. At 1,400 per tonne, the best plan changes to four launches and one elevator tonne, costing 41,400. The exact switching price is 10,000/9, approximately 1,111.11, per tonne. There, three plans tie at 370,000/9: two launches with 19 tonnes, three launches with 10 tonnes, and four launches with one tonne. Unused rocket capacity is permitted, and extra launches are chosen only when they lower total cost.

Please treat these figures as planning results, not launch-performance guarantees.

Sincerely,
Modeling Team

data_semantics.eliminated_zero: A spreadsheet zero after elimination is a structural status placeholder, not an observed zero-support measurement.
data_semantics.future_na: NA means a future week was not held; it is not an observed support value and carries no evidence for or against either contestant.

inference.results_paragraph: Week 1 yields p_A=0.55 exactly from the supplied combined score. In the independent rank-only week with j_A=0.4 and alpha=0.6, s_A=0.24+0.4p_A and s_B=1-s_A, so the official strict combined-score ranking requires p_A>0.65; the feasibility set is 0.65<p_A<=1. For always_wins, s_A=0.72+0.2p_A exceeds 0.5 for every p_A in [0,1], so both endpoints are feasible. For impossible_win, s_A=0.14+0.3p_A is at most 0.44, so A can never strictly outrank B; the feasibility set is empty. These rank results are deterministic feasibility sets, not confidence intervals. No total votes, sampling distribution, or repeated observations were supplied, so absolute vote counts are not identifiable and no confidence interval is available. A spreadsheet zero after elimination is a status placeholder, not evidence of zero support; NA for a future week means the week was not held and provides no support information.
